---
title: "Session 5: Visualising with ggplot2 (and maps)"
subtitle: "From the grammar of graphics to a choropleth of the world, with the World Bank data"
---

::: {.objectifs}
Session objectives

- Read any ggplot as a stack of layers: data, aesthetics, geoms, scales, labels, theme.
- Build the classic "Gapminder" scatter: life expectancy against income, with log scales and readable labels.
- Choose the right chart: line (change over time), bar (comparison), histogram and boxplot (distribution).
- Apply the "signal vs context" principle: highlight one series, grey out the others.
- Draw a world map with `sf`, join it safely to the WDI data, and check what did not match.
- Save a figure with explicit size and resolution.
:::

::: {.prepare}
Prepare your R session

**Packages used today:** `tidyverse`, `scales`, `ggrepel`, `sf`, `rnaturalearth`, `rnaturalearthdata`, `here`. Install any that are missing with `install.packages()`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")   # R messages in English

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(ggrepel)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(here)

source(here("R", "theme_cours.R"))   # theme_cours(), pal_cours, pal_regions

wdi <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# One row per country for one year: the cross-section used below
wdi_2022 <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2022)
```

**Script of this session:** [download seance-5.R](../scripts/seance-5.R){download="seance-5.R"}, all the code of this page in one file.
:::

Everything in this session uses the full panel (`wdi`, about 217 countries, 2000-2023). When a chart needs **one point per country**, we take one year, 2022 (`wdi_2022`). This matters: a common mistake is to draw a histogram on pooled years (for instance 63 values from three countries). A chart is only as good as the question its data answer.

Why 2022? It is the latest year with good coverage for the variables we use (2023 has many more missing values). Session 4 used 2019, the last pre-COVID year, because it studied a relationship, not the present.

**Pacing.** The core path takes about 180 minutes, exercises included. Parts marked **Optional: going further** (the annotation part of Exercise 5.5, and Exercise 5.6) add about 20 minutes: do them if time allows, or at home.

## Check extremes before plotting (≈ 5 min)

Before drawing anything, look at the extremes: one absurd value stretches an axis and hides everything else.

```{r}
#| label: check-extremes
wdi_2022 |>
  drop_na(life_exp) |>
  slice_min(life_exp, n = 3) |>
  select(country, iso3c, life_exp)
```

The Central African Republic shows a life expectancy of `r nb(min(wdi_2022$life_exp, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` years in 2022. The next lowest country is at about `r nb(sort(wdi_2022$life_exp)[2], 0)`. This value is implausible: it is a data artefact, not a finding. As Session 4 showed, it is not a one-year glitch: the whole CAF life-expectancy series is unreliable in this WDI release (it also reads 14.7 years in 2009). We never edit the raw file; we **exclude the series explicitly, for every year, and say so**, with the same line as in Session 4. Setting only `life_exp` to `NA` keeps the country's other variables (for example electricity access, used in the map below).

```{r}
#| label: fix-caf
# CAF life expectancy is unreliable in this WDI release (14.7 in 2009, 18.8 in 2022): exclude every year
wdi <- wdi |> mutate(life_exp = if_else(iso3c == "CAF", NA_real_, life_exp))

wdi_2022 <- filter(wdi, year == 2022)
```

## The grammar of graphics

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can read any ggplot as a stack of layers and build one step by step.
:::

A ggplot is not a "chart type". It is a **recipe** with independent ingredients, added with `+`:

| Ingredient | Question it answers | Typical code |
|---|---|---|
| **data** | Which table? | `ggplot(data = wdi_2022)` |
| **aes**thetics | Which variable goes to which visual channel (x, y, colour, size)? | `aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)` |
| **geom** | Which shape draws the data? | `geom_point()` |
| **scales** | How is a value translated into a position / colour / size? | `scale_x_log10()`, `scale_colour_manual()` |
| **labs** | What does the reader see in words? | `labs(title = , x = , y = , caption = )` |
| **theme** | How does everything non-data look? | `theme_cours()` |

::: {.definition}
**Aesthetic**: a visual channel (x, y, colour, fill, size, shape) that you link to a variable inside `aes()`. **Geom**: the shape that draws the data (point, line, bar...). **Scale**: the rule that translates a data value into a position or a colour. **Facet**: a small multiple, the same chart repeated for each group.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  A[data] --> B[aes]
  B --> C[geom]
  C --> D[scales]
  D --> E[labs]
  E --> F[theme]
```

The rule to remember: **aesthetics map variables, arguments set constants**. `aes(colour = region)` colours by the data; `colour = "red"` outside `aes()` paints everything red.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea

A ggplot is built by **adding layers with `+`**. You never ask for "a scatter plot": you give data, say which variables go where, and choose a shape. Everything else (scales, labels, theme) refines the result.
:::

Let us build one plot, one ingredient at a time. Steps 1 to 4 are shown side by side so you can see what each `+` adds; step 5 is the finished figure.

:::: {layout-ncol=2}
```{r}
#| label: layer-1
#| fig-alt: "Empty chart canvas with a horizontal axis for GDP per capita and a vertical axis for life expectancy. No data are drawn yet."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Step 1. Data and aesthetics only: an empty canvas with axes."
wdi_2022_ok <- wdi_2022 |>
  drop_na(gdp_pc_ppp, life_exp)        # a point needs both coordinates

ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp))
```

```{r}
#| label: layer-2
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of life expectancy against GDP per capita, one point per country. Life expectancy rises steeply at low incomes, then levels off."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Step 2. Add a geom: now the data are drawn."
ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
#| label: layer-3
#| fig-alt: "Same scatter plot with a logarithmic x axis and dollar labels. The points now form a roughly straight upward band."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Step 3. Add a scale: logarithmic x axis with dollar labels."
ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()))
```

```{r}
#| label: layer-4
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of life expectancy against log GDP per capita, points coloured by region. Regions cluster: Sub-Saharan Africa at the lower left, Europe at the upper right."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Step 4. Map one more variable: colour by region (new aesthetic, new scale)."
ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, guide = "none")
```
::::

In step 2 most countries are squeezed on the left: income is very skewed, so a log scale (step 3) spreads them out. In step 4 the legend is hidden only to keep the small panel readable; step 5 brings it back.

**Step 5.** Labels and theme: the message in the title, units on the axes, the source.

```{r}
#| label: layer-5
#| fig-alt: "Final scatter plot of life expectancy against log GDP per capita, coloured by region, with title, axis labels, legend and source. Richer countries live longer, but gains flatten at the top."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 4, title.position = "top")) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Richer countries live longer, but gains flatten at the top", 60),
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    colour = "Region",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022."
  ) +
  theme_cours(base_size = 11)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `theme_cours()` already applies

`R/theme_cours.R` calls `theme_set(theme_cours())`, so every plot uses the course theme by default. Writing `+ theme_cours(base_size = 11)` is only needed to change an argument (here, smaller text for small figures).
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

Writing `aes(colour = "red")` instead of `colour = "red"`. Inside `aes()`, `"red"` is treated as a *variable* with one value, so ggplot invents a legend and picks its own colour (salmon, not red). **Fixed colour: outside `aes()`. Colour by data: inside `aes()`.**
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## In plain words

Think of a ggplot as a sandwich: the data is the bread, each `+` adds a filling. You can add or remove one filling without rebuilding the rest.
:::

## The Gapminder scatter

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can combine four variables on one chart and label a few points without clutter.
:::

This is the figure that made Hans Rosling famous: income, health, population and region on one plot. We add a fourth variable (population, as point **size**) and label a few countries with `ggrepel`, which moves labels so they do not overlap.

```{r}
#| label: gapminder
#| fig-alt: "Bubble chart of life expectancy against log GDP per capita; bubble size is population, colour is region. China, India, Nigeria and the United States are labelled. Similar incomes can hide a 20-year gap."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
focus <- c("China", "India", "Nigeria", "United States")

ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = population, colour = region), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = filter(wdi_2022_ok, country %in% focus),
    aes(label = country),
    min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 1, point.padding = 0.5, seed = 1, size = 4.2,
    bg.color = "white", bg.r = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 14, breaks = c(1e7, 1e8, 1e9),
                  labels = c("10 M", "100 M", "1 B")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3, title.position = "top", order = 1,
                               override.aes = list(size = 4)),
         size = guide_legend(title.position = "top", order = 2)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
        legend.box.just = "left", legend.spacing.y = unit(2, "pt")) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Income and life expectancy rise together, but similar incomes can hide a 20-year gap", 60),
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    colour = "Region", size = "Population",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. One point per country; countries with missing data are dropped.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart

- Each bubble is a country. **Higher** means longer life, **further right** means richer, **bigger** means more people.
- The cloud rises fast on the left and flattens on the right: an extra \$10,000 matters a lot at \$2,000, little at \$40,000.
- At the same income, countries can differ by about 20 years: income is far from the whole story.
:::

Reading tips:

- The **x axis is logarithmic**: equal distances mean equal *percentage* differences in income. A move from \$2,000 to \$4,000 counts as much as from \$20,000 to \$40,000.
- `scale_size_area()` makes the *area* proportional to population. The default `scale_size()` is also area-based but does not start at zero, which exaggerates small countries.
- `geom_text_repel(data = ...)` takes **its own data**: only the four focus countries are labelled, the rest of the plot is unchanged. This is how you label a few points without clutter.
- A **scale** is the rule from value to visual channel; `scale_size_area()` is the scale of the `size` aesthetic, `scale_x_log10()` that of `x`.
- This is a cross-section, not a causal result: richer countries differ in many other ways (institutions, climate, disease burden). The curve describes, it does not say that money *causes* longevity.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

**Colour vs fill.** `colour` paints outlines and points; `fill` paints areas (bars, boxes, polygons). Using `colour = region` on `geom_col()` gives coloured outlines and grey bars: switch to `fill`. For `geom_point()` the default shape has no inside, so `colour` is the right one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 5.1

Using `wdi_2022_ok`, draw a scatter of life expectancy (y) against **electricity access** (x, % of population), coloured by `income` group. Drop missing values first, give it a message title and labelled axes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| label: ex-5-1
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of life expectancy against the share of the population with electricity access, coloured by income group. Countries without universal access have markedly lower life expectancy."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
wdi_2022 |>
  drop_na(elec_access, life_exp, income) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = elec_access, y = life_exp, colour = income)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = "%")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Low income" = "#D55E00", "Lower middle income" = "#E69F00",
                                 "Upper middle income" = "#56B4E9", "High income" = "#0072B2")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Countries without universal electricity have markedly lower life expectancy", 60),
    x = "Population with access to electricity (%)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    colour = "Income group (current World Bank classification)",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022.", 95)
  )
```
:::

## Lines: change over time

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can draw a time series that highlights one country and labels lines directly.
:::

Before choosing a geom, ask which question you are answering:

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea: which chart for which question?

| Your question | Chart | Geom |
|---|---|---|
| Compare groups or countries | bars | `geom_col()`, `geom_bar()` |
| How is one variable spread? | histogram, density, boxplot | `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()`, `geom_boxplot()` |
| Are two variables related? | scatter plot | `geom_point()` |
| How does it evolve over time? | line | `geom_line()` |
| Where is it? | map | `geom_sf()` |
:::

A line connects observations **in a meaningful order** (here, years) for the **same unit** (here, a country). You must tell ggplot which points belong together with `group` (or with `colour`, which groups implicitly).

The dataviz principle of the workshop: **signal versus context**. If everything is coloured, nothing stands out. Draw the context in grey first, then the signal on top, in colour.

```{r}
#| label: lines
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of life expectancy from 2000 to 2023 for eight countries. India is a thick red line, the seven others thin grey lines. India gained nine years; of the eight countries, only Bangladesh gained more (about 13 years)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
compare <- c("India", "China", "Nigeria", "Brazil", "United States", "Germany", "Japan", "Bangladesh")
highlight <- "India"

life_lines <- wdi |>
  filter(country %in% compare) |>
  drop_na(life_exp)

ggplot(life_lines, aes(x = year, y = life_exp, group = country)) +
  geom_line(data = filter(life_lines, country != highlight),
            colour = pal_cours[["gris"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = filter(life_lines, country == highlight),
            colour = pal_cours[["accent"]], linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(life_lines, year == max(year)),
                  aes(label = country, colour = country == highlight),
                  hjust = 0, direction = "y", xlim = c(2023.4, NA), size = 4,
                  segment.color = NA, show.legend = FALSE, seed = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal_cours[["accent"]], `FALSE` = "grey40")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2020, 5), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2000, 2027), clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("India gained nine years of life expectancy since 2000; of these eight countries, only Bangladesh gained more", 60),
    x = "Year",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. India in red; seven comparison countries in grey.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart

- The **red line** is the signal (India); the grey lines are context. Compare the *slopes*, not only the endpoints.
- Lines that rise steadily mean steady gains; the small dip around 2020-2021 is a shock shared by several countries.
- Names at the right end replace the legend: follow a line to its label.
:::

Points to notice:

- Two `geom_line()` layers, each with its own `data`: grey context first, red signal on top.
- Labels sit at the **end of the lines** (`year == max(year)`), so no legend is needed. Direct labelling is faster to read than a legend.
- `coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)` leaves room on the right for the labels, and `geom_text_repel(direction = "y")` pushes them apart vertically so they do not overlap.
- The 2020-2021 dip is visible for several countries: COVID-19 excess mortality.
- In current ggplot2 the line width argument is `linewidth =` (not `size =`).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 5.2

For each region, compute the **median life expectancy** per year (use `wdi`). Draw one line per region with the colours of `pal_regions`, labelled directly at the right end (no legend). Title: the message.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| label: ex-5-2
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of median life expectancy by region from 2000 to 2023, one coloured line per region, labelled at the right. Sub-Saharan Africa gained 12 years but still trails every other region."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
life_region <- wdi |>
  drop_na(life_exp) |>
  summarise(life_med = median(life_exp), .by = c(region, year))

ggplot(life_region, aes(x = year, y = life_med, colour = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = filter(life_region, year == max(year)),
    aes(label = str_wrap(region, 20)),
    hjust = 0, direction = "y", xlim = c(2023.4, NA), size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.85,
    segment.color = NA, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2020, 5), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.05))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2000, 2028), clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Sub-Saharan Africa gained 12 years since 2000 but still trails every other region", 60),
    x = "Year",
    y = "Median life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. Median across countries of each region (countries are not weighted by population).", 95)
  )
```
:::

## Bars: comparing groups

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can pick `geom_col()` or `geom_bar()` and produce honest, sorted bar charts.
:::

Two different bar charts, two different geoms:

| You have... | Use | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| raw rows, you want **counts** | `geom_bar()` | counts rows for you |
| an already computed number per group | `geom_col()` | uses your `y` as the bar height |

(A common mistake is `geom_bar(stat = "identity")`. `geom_col()` is the same thing, clearer.)

### Values: median GDP per capita by region, sorted

Two rules for bar charts: start at **zero**, and **sort** the bars. For text categories, put the long labels on the vertical axis (horizontal bars). `fct_reorder()` sorts a factor by another variable.

```{r}
#| label: bars-col
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of median GDP per capita by region, bars sorted from lowest to highest with dollar values at the tips. North America is about seven times above South Asia."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
gdp_region <- wdi_2022_ok |>
  summarise(gdp_med = median(gdp_pc_ppp), n_countries = n(), .by = region)

gdp_region |>
  mutate(region = fct_reorder(region, gdp_med)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_med, y = region)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_cours[["principal"]], width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_dollar(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale())(gdp_med)), hjust = -0.1, size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = label_wrap(28)) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("A typical North American country is about seven times richer than one in South Asia", 60),
    x = "Median GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. Median across countries; North America has only 3 countries.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

**Truncated bar axes.** A bar encodes a value by its *length*, so the axis must start at zero. Starting at 50 makes a difference of 10% look like a difference of 100%. If zero is not meaningful, use points or lines instead of bars. (Same logic: do not use 3D bars and do not leave bars in alphabetical order when the values can be ranked.)
:::

### Counts: number of countries by income group

The `income` column is the **income group (current World Bank classification)**: each country's group today, applied to every year (see Session 4). The World Bank sets these groups from gross national income per capita (Atlas method, current US$), not from the GDP per capita in PPP that we plot.

Income groups have a natural order (low to high), so we turn the column into an **ordered factor** by hand. Alphabetical order would put "High income" first.

```{r}
#| label: bars-count
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of the number of countries in each World Bank income group, with counts above the bars. High-income countries are the largest group, and 25 countries are low-income."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
niveaux <- c("Low income", "Lower middle income", "Upper middle income", "High income")

wdi_2022 |>
  mutate(income = factor(income, levels = niveaux, ordered = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income)) +
  geom_bar(fill = pal_cours[["principal"]], width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = after_stat(count)), stat = "count", vjust = -0.4, size = 4.5) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = label_wrap(14)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("High-income countries are the largest group, but 25 countries are still low-income", 60),
    x = "Income group (current World Bank classification)",
    y = "Number of countries",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. All economies in the WDI panel.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 5.3

Show the **ten richest countries** in 2022 (GDP per capita, PPP) as sorted horizontal bars. Use `slice_max()`, not `top_n()` (superseded). Colour the bars by region with `pal_regions`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| label: ex-5-3
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of GDP per capita for the ten richest countries, coloured by region and sorted by value. Nine are small economies or financial centres, such as Singapore, Luxembourg, Ireland, Qatar and Bermuda; the United States, tenth, is the only large economy."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
wdi_2022_ok |>
  slice_max(gdp_pc_ppp, n = 10) |>
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, gdp_pc_ppp)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = country, fill = region)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 4)) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Nine of the ten richest countries are small economies or financial centres; the United States is the exception", 60),
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)",
    y = NULL, fill = "Region",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022.", 95)
  )
```
:::

## Distributions

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can show how a variable is spread across countries, overall and by group.
:::

To see how a variable is spread **across countries**, use one observation per country: `wdi_2022_ok`. (Pooling all years would count each country 24 times, and the observations would not be independent.)

### Histogram and density

GDP per capita is very right-skewed, so we work on a **log scale**. We pick the bin width on that scale (here `bins = 25`) and compare a few values: too few bins hide structure, too many show noise. Putting the histogram on the *density* scale lets us overlay a smooth density curve.

```{r}
#| label: histogram
#| fig-alt: "Histogram with a red density curve of GDP per capita across countries on a log x axis. Incomes span more than a 100-fold range, with no single typical country."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 25,
                 fill = pal_cours[["principal"]], alpha = 0.6, colour = "white") +
  geom_density(colour = pal_cours[["accent"]], linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("World incomes span more than a 100-fold range, with no single typical country", 60),
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $, log scale)",
    y = "Density",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. One observation per country; red line = kernel density estimate.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart

- Each bar counts the countries in one slice of the (log) income axis: tall bars are common incomes.
- The red density line smooths the bars. Two humps would mean two groups of countries; here the mass is spread over a wide range.
- Because the axis is logarithmic, the same width means the same *percentage* gap, not the same dollar gap.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

**Linear scale on skewed data.** On a linear axis, a few rich countries stretch the range and nearly all others pile up on the left. Try `scale_x_log10()` for incomes, populations and any quantity spanning orders of magnitude, and say on the axis title that it is a log scale.
:::

### Boxplot by group

A boxplot shows the median (line), the middle half of observations (box) and unusual values (points). Add the individual countries with a light jitter, so the reader sees how many observations sit behind each box.

```{r}
#| label: boxplot
#| fig-alt: "Boxplots of GDP per capita (log scale) for each income group (current World Bank classification), with individual countries as dots. The median rises from about $2,500 in the low-income group to about $49,000 in the high-income group, but neighbouring groups overlap and each spans a wide range of incomes."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
wdi_2022_ok |>
  mutate(income = factor(income, levels = niveaux, ordered = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = gdp_pc_ppp)) +
  geom_boxplot(outliers = FALSE, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey30", width = 0.55) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, colour = pal_cours[["principal"]], size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = label_wrap(14)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Median income rises steeply from one income group to the next, but neighbouring groups overlap", 60),
    x = "Income group (current World Bank classification)",
    y = str_wrap("GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $, log scale)", 40),
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. Box = quartiles and median; dots = individual countries.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

**Too many colours.** Colouring by 7 regions plus a gradient plus size makes a chart nobody can decode. Use colour for one idea; grey for the rest. If you need more than about 6 colours, facet or highlight instead.
:::

Why `outliers = FALSE`? Otherwise the boxplot draws the outliers *and* the jitter draws them again.

The groups overlap because they are not defined on this axis: the World Bank classifies countries by gross national income per capita, not GDP per capita in PPP, and `income` holds today's group, not the 2022 one. The richest low-income country (`r nb_dollar(max(wdi_2022_ok$gdp_pc_ppp[wdi_2022_ok$income == "Low income"]))`) is richer than the poorest upper-middle-income one (`r nb_dollar(min(wdi_2022_ok$gdp_pc_ppp[wdi_2022_ok$income == "Upper middle income"]))`).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 5.4

Compare the distribution of life expectancy in **2000 and 2022**. Use `facet_wrap(~ year)` on a histogram of life expectancy (one observation per country). What happened to the left tail?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| label: ex-5-4
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side histograms of life expectancy across countries, for 2000 and 2022. The low-life-expectancy tail shrank between the two years."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
wdi |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2022)) |>
  drop_na(life_exp) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = life_exp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5, fill = pal_cours[["principal"]], colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("The low-life-expectancy tail shrank between 2000 and 2022", 60),
    x = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    y = "Number of countries",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000 and 2022. One observation per country and year.", 95)
  )
```

In 2000, `r nb(sum(wdi$life_exp[wdi$year == 2000] < 55, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` countries had a life expectancy below 55 years; in 2022 only `r nb(sum(wdi$life_exp[wdi$year == 2022] < 55, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` do (the Central African Republic series is excluded, see the start of this page). The whole distribution shifted to the right.
:::

## Maps

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 40 min]{.duration} After this section you can draw a choropleth of the world, join it safely to the WDI data and check what did not match.
:::

::: {.definition}
**Choropleth**: a map where each area is coloured according to a value. **`sf` (simple features)**: the R format that stores shapes as a `geometry` column in a data frame.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  A[Shapes: Natural Earth] --> C[left_join on iso code]
  B[Data: WDI 2022] --> C
  C --> D[anti_join check]
  D --> E[bin values]
  E --> F[geom_sf + projection]
```

A choropleth colours areas by a value. A good one needs four things: **all** the geometries, a **safe join**, a **readable scale**, and an honest **projection**. A common mistake is to colour only a handful of countries, because the join was done on country names and kept only the matching rows.

### 1. Geometries: one row per country, in an `sf` table

`sf` ("simple features") stores each country's shape in a `geometry` column. The result behaves like a data frame: `dplyr` verbs work on it.

```{r}
#| label: ne-load
world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
  filter(name != "Antarctica")          # no data there, and it eats a fifth of the map

dim(world)
world |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(name, iso_a3, iso_a3_eh, adm0_a3) |>
  slice(1:5)
```

Natural Earth has several ISO-like codes. Which one matches the WDI `iso3c`? Do not guess: **test with `anti_join()`**, which keeps the rows of the left table that find no match.

```{r}
#| label: join-check
# WDI countries with no match in the map, for each candidate code
unmatched <- function(code) {
  wdi_2022 |>
    anti_join(st_drop_geometry(world), by = c("iso3c" = code)) |>
    pull(country)
}

# How many WDI economies stay unmatched with each code?
length(unmatched("iso_a3"))
length(unmatched("iso_a3_eh"))
length(unmatched("adm0_a3"))

unmatched("iso_a3_eh")
```

`iso_a3_eh` is the best key: only a few WDI economies are missing from the map. They are small or disputed territories (Channel Islands, Gibraltar, Kosovo, which has a non-standard code in Natural Earth). The reverse check shows map areas without WDI data:

```{r}
#| label: join-check-reverse
world |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  anti_join(wdi_2022, by = c("iso_a3_eh" = "iso3c")) |>
  select(name, iso_a3_eh) |>
  head(8)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why it matters for development economics

Here the losses are small: three small or disputed territories on the WDI side, and mostly tiny territories without WDI data on the map side. That is because we join on codes. A join on country names would leave about 50 WDI economies without a shape, among them the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Yemen and Côte d'Ivoire, and the map would show them as "no data" without any warning. Checking the join is part of measuring development honestly.
:::

Never join on country *names*: "Russian Federation" (WDI) is "Russia" (Natural Earth), "Egypt, Arab Rep." is "Egypt". Codes are far more stable than names, though they do change (ROM became ROU, ZAR became COD): run `anti_join()` anyway.

### 2. Join and plot

We start from the **map** (`left_join(world, data)`) so that every country keeps its shape, even without data. Those get `NA` and will be drawn in light grey.

```{r}
#| label: map-join
world_gdp <- world |>
  select(iso_a3_eh, geometry) |>
  left_join(select(wdi_2022, iso3c, country, gdp_pc_ppp, elec_access),
            by = c("iso_a3_eh" = "iso3c"))

sum(is.na(world_gdp$gdp_pc_ppp))   # shapes drawn in grey (no data)
```

GDP per capita is skewed, so a continuous colour scale would make almost everything look the same. We **bin** the values into classes with round breakpoints and readable labels.

```{r}
#| label: map-gdp
#| fig-alt: "World map in the Robinson projection, countries shaded in six classes of GDP per capita, light grey where there is no data. Income is highest in the North and lowest in Sub-Saharan Africa."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.8
cuts   <- c(0, 2500, 5000, 10000, 20000, 40000, Inf)
labs_g <- c("< $2,500", "$2,500-5,000", "$5,000-10,000", "$10,000-20,000",
            "$20,000-40,000", "> $40,000")

world_gdp |>
  mutate(gdp_class = cut(gdp_pc_ppp, breaks = cuts, labels = labs_g, right = FALSE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fct_na_value_to_level(gdp_class, "No data")),   # NA becomes a level
          colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(hcl.colors(6, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE), "grey85"),  # one colour per level, in order
                    drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, title.position = "top")) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    title = str_wrap("Income per head is highest in the North and lowest in Sub-Saharan Africa", 60),
    fill = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. Light grey: no data.", 95)
  ) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey94"))
```

What makes this map honest:

- **All countries** are drawn. Missing data get their own level, "No data", in light grey: `fct_na_value_to_level()` turns `NA` into a real factor level, the last one, so that it appears in the legend. `scale_fill_manual()` then gives one colour per level, in the order of the levels (`drop = FALSE` keeps every level, even an empty one, so colours cannot shift).
- **Binned scale** with round breaks and labels written in dollars, not `1e+04`.
- **`coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin")`**: Robinson projection, a compromise that distorts areas less than the default longitude/latitude rectangle. A string like `"+proj=robin"` is a PROJ definition; `"EPSG:4326"` would give plain lat/long.
- Area is not population: Russia and Canada look large, India small. A choropleth of an *intensive* variable (per capita) is fair; one of *totals* would mislead.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 5.5

Map **access to electricity** (% of population) in 2022 for all countries, in bins (for example below 50%, 50-80%, 80-99%, 99-100%).

**Optional: going further.** Then **annotate the three countries with the lowest access**, with their names and values. Hint: use `slice_min()` to find them and `st_point_on_surface()` for a label position inside each country. (We use the lowest, not the highest: more than 100 countries are at 100%, so "top 3" would be an arbitrary tie.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| label: ex-5-5
#| fig-alt: "World map shaded by four classes of electricity access, with the three lowest-access countries (South Sudan, Burundi, Chad) labelled by name and value. Twenty of the 22 countries where less than half the population has electricity are in Sub-Saharan Africa."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.8
bottom3 <- world_gdp |>
  drop_na(elec_access) |>
  slice_min(elec_access, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(str_remove(country, ",.*"), " ", round(elec_access), "%")) |>
  st_point_on_surface()                       # one point inside each polygon

bottom3$label                                  # check which countries are annotated

world_gdp |>
  mutate(elec_class = cut(elec_access, breaks = c(0, 50, 80, 99, 100.01),
                          labels = c("< 50%", "50-80%", "80-99%", "99-100%"),
                          right = FALSE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fct_na_value_to_level(elec_class, "No data")),
          colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_label_repel(data = bottom3, aes(label = label, geometry = geometry),
                   stat = "sf_coordinates", size = 3.4, fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   min.segment.length = Inf, box.padding = 0.2, seed = 1) +  # no leader lines
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#08306b", "#2171b5", "#9ecae1", "#eff3ff", "grey85"),  # in level order
                    drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, title.position = "top")) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    title = str_wrap("20 of the 22 countries where less than half the population has electricity are in Sub-Saharan Africa", 60),
    fill = "Population with access to electricity",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. Labels (placed near the countries): the three with the lowest access. Light grey: no data.", 95)
  ) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey94"))
```
:::

## Saving figures

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 10 min]{.duration} After this section you can export a figure with a fixed size and resolution.
:::

In a report, the figure on screen is not the figure in the file. Save with **explicit size and resolution** so the output is identical on every computer. Store the plot in an object, then call `ggsave()`.

```{r}
#| label: save
#| eval: false
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)   # output/ is created if missing

p_gapminder <- ggplot(wdi_2022_ok, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, colour = region)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()))

ggsave(here("output", "gapminder.png"), plot = p_gapminder,
       width = 8, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300)    # for Word / slides
ggsave(here("output", "gapminder.pdf"), plot = p_gapminder,
       width = 8, height = 5)                             # vector, for LaTeX
```

- `width` and `height` are in inches (`units = "cm"` is possible). Choose them to match the final placement; do not resize in Word.
- 300 dpi is the standard for print; 150 is enough for the web.
- Without `plot =`, `ggsave()` saves the **last plot displayed**, which is fragile in a script.
- `here()` builds the path from the project root, so the code runs on any machine.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea

A figure is a **deliverable**: message in the title, units on the axes, source in the caption, fixed size on export. If the title says nothing, the reader has to do your analysis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 5.6 (Optional: going further)

Make a boxplot of **life expectancy by region** (2022, one point per country), regions sorted by median, horizontal, and save it as a 300 dpi PNG in `output/`. The save chunk must not be evaluated when the page is rendered.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| label: ex-5-6
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal boxplots of life expectancy by region, sorted by median. Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest median, about 9 years below the next region."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
p_life_region <- wdi_2022 |>
  drop_na(life_exp) |>
  mutate(region = fct_reorder(region, life_exp, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = life_exp, y = region)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey92", colour = "grey30", width = 0.55) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = label_wrap(28)) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest median life expectancy, about 9 years below the next region", 60),
    x = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. One observation per country.", 95)
  )

p_life_region
```

```{r}
#| label: ex-5-6-save
#| eval: false
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(here("output", "life_exp_region.png"), plot = p_life_region,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```
:::

## Key takeaways

- A ggplot is a stack of independent layers: data, aesthetics, geoms, scales, labels, theme. Learn the grammar, not the recipes.
- `aes()` maps variables; arguments outside `aes()` set constants.
- Log scales and `scales::label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())` / `label_number()` make skewed development data readable. Never leave `1e+04` on an axis.
- Title = the message; axes with units; caption with the source. Direct labels beat legends.
- Highlight one series in colour and grey out the rest (signal vs context). Sort bars, start them at zero, use `geom_col()` for values and `geom_bar()` for counts.
- For distributions, use one observation per country; do not pool years and call them independent.
- Maps: keep all shapes, join on **codes** (not names), check with `anti_join()`, bin skewed values, use a projection, grey for missing data.
- Save with `ggsave()` and explicit `width`, `height`, `dpi`.
